fathers/gregory-of-nazianzus/summary: Gregory of Nazianzus (c. 329–390), ‘the Theologian’, the greatest orator of the Greek church, preached the Five Theological Orations in Constantinople in 380, openly confessing the Holy Spirit as God, presided briefly over the Council of 381 and resigned, leaving the classic formulations of Trinitarian and Christological orthodoxy.
fathers/gregory-of-nazianzus/story:
Gregory was born around 329 at Arianzus near Nazianzus in south-west Cappadocia, son of Gregory the Elder, bishop of Nazianzus, and the devout Nonna. He studied at Caesarea in Palestine, Alexandria and for nearly ten years at Athens, where he and Basil were inseparable friends; he later said they knew only two roads, one to the church and the other to the schools.

Torn all his life between contemplative retirement and public ministry, he was ordained presbyter by his father against his will (361), fled, and returned to write his Apology for his Flight (Oration 2), a classic on the burdens of the priesthood used by Chrysostom and Gregory the Great. In 372 Basil, needing allies against Valens, consecrated him bishop of the tiny post-town of Sasima, which he never occupied; the episode embittered their friendship.

In 379, after Valens’ death, the small Nicene community of Constantinople invited him to the capital, where the churches were in Homoian hands. Preaching in a private chapel he named the Anastasia (‘Resurrection’), he delivered in 380 the five Theological Orations (27–31), defending the full divinity of Son and Spirit against Eunomians and ‘Spirit-fighters’ (Pneumatomachi). He stated plainly what Basil had avoided: ‘Is the Spirit God? Most certainly. Is he consubstantial? Yes, if he is God’ (Oration 31.10). He explained the persons by their relations — unbegotten, begotten, proceeding — and the gradual revelation of the Trinity in scripture.

When Theodosius I expelled the Homoian bishop, Gregory was enthroned in the Church of the Holy Apostles, and in 381 he presided over the Council of Constantinople after the death of Meletius. Opposed over the Antiochene succession and challenged on the canonical legitimacy of his translation from another see, he resigned with a bitter farewell oration (Oration 42) and returned to Cappadocia. There he administered Nazianzus for a time, wrote against Apollinarius (Letters 101–102 to Cledonius: ‘what has not been assumed has not been healed’) and composed some 17,000 lines of poetry, including the autobiographical De vita sua. He died around 390.

Gregory’s orations became the most copied texts in Byzantium after the Bible and the core of Byzantine rhetorical education; Byzantine commentators such as Maximus the Confessor wrote on his ‘difficult passages’ (Ambigua). Only John the Evangelist and Symeon the New Theologian share his title ‘the Theologian’ in Orthodox tradition.
fathers/gregory-of-nazianzus/roots/0/tex: Trained under the sophists Himerius and Prohaeresius at Athens, he fused Christian theology with the full artistry of Greek oratory; Julian’s ban on Christian teachers (362) provoked his Invectives against Julian.
fathers/gregory-of-nazianzus/roots/1/tex: Co-editor of the Philokalia of Origen; dependent on Athanasius, whom he eulogised in Oration 21, and on Basil.
fathers/gregory-of-nazianzus/roots/2/tex: His language of God as light, of purification preceding contemplation and of the limits of human knowledge draws on Plato and Plotinus.
fathers/gregory-of-nazianzus/roots/3/tex: His account of Moses entering the cloud on Sinai (Oration 28.3) frames the knowledge of God as partial and given.
fathers/gregory-of-nazianzus/roots/4/tex: His brief episcopate in Constantinople depended on Theodosius’ enforcement of Nicene orthodoxy (edict Cunctos populos, 380).
fathers/gregory-of-nazianzus/keyTeaching: The Holy Spirit is God and consubstantial with the Father
The persons are distinguished by relations: unbegottenness, begottenness and procession
‘What has not been assumed has not been healed’: Christ had a full human mind and soul, against Apollinarius
The knowledge of God requires purification; God’s essence remains incomprehensible
Progressive revelation: the Old Testament proclaimed the Father, the New the Son, and the church now experiences the Spirit
Mary is Theotokos; whoever denies this is ‘severed from the Godhead’
fathers/gregory-of-nazianzus/works/0/not: Five sermons on God, the Son and the Spirit, delivered in Constantinople.
fathers/gregory-of-nazianzus/works/2/not: Epiphany sermon on baptism, delivered in Constantinople.
fathers/gregory-of-nazianzus/works/3/not: Treatise on the priesthood and pastoral care.
fathers/gregory-of-nazianzus/works/4/tit: De vita sua and other poems
fathers/gregory-of-nazianzus/works/4/not: Autobiographical verse; around 17,000 lines of poetry in all.
fathers/gregory-of-nazianzus/doctrineCon: The clearest Cappadocian statement of the Spirit’s divinity and of the relational distinction of persons.
Openly confessed the Spirit as God and homoousios, going beyond the reticence of Basil and of the creed of 381.
The soteriological axiom ‘the unassumed is unhealed’ became decisive against Apollinarianism and for later Christology.
His orations on Epiphany and baptism shaped Byzantine baptismal theology.
An early strong defender of the title Theotokos.
fathers/gregory-of-nazianzus/laterInflue: His orations were the most copied Byzantine texts after scripture, commented on by Maximus the Confessor and read in schools.
Phrases from his Christmas and Easter orations were turned into hymns by Cosmas of Maiuma and John of Damascus.
Rufinus translated nine orations; Aquinas and medieval theologians cited him as ‘Gregorius Theologus’.
Central to 20th-century relational accounts of the Trinity, from Zizioulas to T. F. Torrance.
fathers/gregory-of-nazianzus/reception/0: ‘The Theologian’, one of the Three Holy Hierarchs (30 January); personal feast 25 January.
fathers/gregory-of-nazianzus/reception/1: Saint and Doctor of the Church (1568); feast 2 January with Basil.
fathers/gregory-of-nazianzus/reception/2: Revered as a great teacher; the Coptic ‘Liturgy of St Gregory’ is attributed to him.
fathers/gregory-of-nazianzus/reception/3: Commemorated (often 2 January or 9 May) as theologian of the Trinity.
fathers/gregory-of-nazianzus/controversi: Ordination to Sasima and rupture with Basil
Canonical objections to his translation to Constantinople (Nicaea canon 15)
Resignation from the Council of 381 amid factional disputes
His sharp criticism of bishops and synods: ‘I have never seen a good end to any council’ (Letter 130)
fathers/gregory-of-nazianzus/quote/text: For that which he has not assumed he has not healed; but that which is united to God is saved.
fathers/basil-the-great/summary: Basil ‘the Great’ (c. 330–379), bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, gave Greek monasticism its rules, built the ‘Basileias’ charitable city, defended the divinity of the Holy Spirit and formulated the distinction between one ousia (essence) and three hypostases that became the language of Trinitarian orthodoxy.
fathers/basil-the-great/story:
Basil was born around 329–330 into a wealthy, devout Christian family of Pontus and Cappadocia: his grandmother Macrina the Elder had been a disciple of Gregory Thaumaturgus, Origen’s pupil, and his siblings included Gregory of Nyssa, Peter of Sebaste and Macrina the Younger. He studied rhetoric in Caesarea, Constantinople and Athens (c. 350–355), where he formed his friendship with Gregory of Nazianzus and met the future emperor Julian.

Returning home to a promising career, he was, by his own account, turned by Macrina and the example of Eustathius of Sebaste towards the ascetic life. After touring monastic centres in Egypt, Palestine, Syria and Mesopotamia, he withdrew to the family estate at Annesi on the river Iris. There, with Gregory of Nazianzus, he compiled the Philokalia of Origen and drafted the moral and ascetic texts that became his Asceticon (the Longer and Shorter Rules), favouring community life over solitary heroics: ‘Whose feet will you wash if you live alone?’

Ordained presbyter, he became bishop of Caesarea and metropolitan of Cappadocia in 370. He resisted the pro-Homoian policy of Emperor Valens, reportedly answering the prefect Modestus with such boldness that the official said no one had ever spoken to him so. In the famine of 368–369 he organised relief, and on the city’s outskirts he built the Basileias — a complex with hospital, hostel, poorhouse and leprosarium — often cited as a landmark in the history of the hospital.

Theologically, Basil wrote Against Eunomius (364) against the Neo-Arian claim that ‘unbegotten’ defines God’s essence, so that the begotten Son must be of a different essence. In On the Holy Spirit (c. 375) he defended the doxology ‘with the Son, together with the Holy Spirit’ and the equal honour of the Spirit, arguing from baptism and from unwritten apostolic tradition, while tactfully avoiding calling the Spirit ‘God’ outright. His letters (especially Letters 214, 236 and the disputed 38) distinguish ousia, what is common, from hypostasis, what is particular — the formula ‘one ousia, three hypostases’.

His Hexaemeron homilies on Genesis 1 combined Greek natural science with scripture, and his Address to Young Men on Greek literature recommended reading pagan authors like a bee taking honey from flowers. He died, probably on 1 January 379 (some scholars argue 377 or 378), shortly before the Council of Constantinople (381) vindicated the theology he had championed. The Liturgy of St Basil, whose anaphora goes back in part to him, is still celebrated in Orthodox and Coptic churches.
fathers/basil-the-great/roots/0/text: Compiled the Philokalia of Origen; the family piety came from Gregory Thaumaturgus via Macrina the Elder; corresponded with Athanasius.
fathers/basil-the-great/roots/1/text: Trained in Athens in the high rhetorical culture of the Second Sophistic; his Address to Young Men defends selective use of Greek literature.
fathers/basil-the-great/roots/2/text: Influenced by Eustathius of Sebaste and by visits to Egyptian and Syrian monks, he reformed asceticism into a disciplined, ecclesial community life.
fathers/basil-the-great/roots/3/text: His distinction between common nature and individual properties draws on Aristotelian and Stoic logic of universals and particulars.
fathers/basil-the-great/roots/4/text: Stoic language of ‘common quality’ and ‘peculiar quality’ shapes his ousia–hypostasis distinction.
fathers/basil-the-great/roots/5/text: His episcopate was defined by resistance to the Homoian religious policy of Valens and by cooperation with imperial officials in charity.
fathers/basil-the-great/keyTeachings/0: God is one ousia (essence) in three hypostases (persons)
fathers/basil-the-great/keyTeachings/1: The Holy Spirit is to be glorified together with Father and Son
fathers/basil-the-great/keyTeachings/2: Unwritten apostolic tradition alongside scripture (On the Holy Spirit 27)
fathers/basil-the-great/keyTeachings/3: Coenobitic monasticism under obedience, in service of the church and the poor
fathers/basil-the-great/keyTeachings/4: Wealth hoarded is theft from the poor (Homily on ‘I will pull down my barns’)
fathers/basil-the-great/keyTeachings/5: Selective, discerning use of pagan learning
fathers/basil-the-great/works/0/title: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
fathers/basil-the-great/works/0/note: Defence of the Spirit’s equal glory, addressed to Amphilochius of Iconium.
fathers/basil-the-great/works/2/note: Nine Lenten homilies on the six days of creation.
fathers/basil-the-great/works/3/note: Foundation of Eastern monastic life; known in the West through Rufinus’ Latin.
fathers/basil-the-great/works/4/note: Over 360 letters on doctrine, church politics, canon law and friendship.
fathers/basil-the-great/works/5/title: Address to Young Men on Greek Literature
fathers/basil-the-great/works/5/note: Classic text on Christian reading of pagan classics.
fathers/basil-the-great/doctrineContribu: Formulated the ousia–hypostasis distinction that defined the Nicene settlement of 381.
Defended the Spirit’s divinity and worship, preparing the creed’s ‘who with the Father and the Son is worshipped and glorified’.
The Liturgy of St Basil remains in use in Byzantine and Coptic churches.
Pioneered institutional Christian charity and a theology of wealth and social justice.
The Hexaemeron set a model for reading Genesis with contemporary science.
fathers/basil-the-great/laterInfluence/0: He is regarded as the father of Eastern coenobitic monasticism; Orthodox monks are often called ‘Basilian’ in the West.
fathers/basil-the-great/laterInfluence/1: The Rule of Benedict commends ‘the Rule of our holy father Basil’ (ch. 73).
fathers/basil-the-great/laterInfluence/2: The Basileias became a model for Byzantine philanthropic institutions.
fathers/basil-the-great/laterInfluence/3: His formula underlies the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed and later Eastern and Western Trinitarian thought.
fathers/basil-the-great/reception/0/text: One of the Three Holy Hierarchs (30 January), with his own feast on 1 January when the Liturgy of St Basil is served.
fathers/basil-the-great/reception/1/text: Saint and Doctor of the Church (declared 1568); feast 2 January with Gregory of Nazianzus.
fathers/basil-the-great/reception/2/text: The Coptic Liturgy of St Basil is the church’s principal eucharistic liturgy.
fathers/basil-the-great/reception/3/text: Commemorated (14 June in many Anglican calendars) as theologian and monastic founder.
fathers/basil-the-great/controversies/0: Break with his early mentor Eustathius of Sebaste over the Holy Spirit
fathers/basil-the-great/controversies/1: Reticence about calling the Spirit ‘God’ explicitly, criticised by contemporaries
fathers/basil-the-great/controversies/2: Strained relations with Rome and Pope Damasus over the Antiochene schism
fathers/basil-the-great/controversies/3: Appointing Gregory of Nazianzus to the unwanted see of Sasima, which damaged their friendship
fathers/basil-the-great/quote/text: The bread you hold back belongs to the hungry; the coat you keep in your closet belongs to the naked.
fathers/basil-the-great/places/3/name: Annesi on the Iris (family estate and monastery)
